I've put off buying this game since release. The reason: the original teaser showed a very gritty very brutal and harsh world. The first gameplay trailer showed it to be "GTA but reskinned to future tech".

But due to a deep sale I gave it a shot.

It's alright. It's definitely entertaining. But it's not the game I was hoping it would be. It's not the "Blade Runner" dark dystopian vibes. It's more "GTA meets Saints Row" vibes. "haha d*ck implants malfunction" vibes. The characters are all caricatures, stereotypes, blown to the extremes. Voice lines sometimes feel like they recorded them out of order over several sessions with no cohesion or flow. You are constantly being slammed by messages and calls and side information but there really isn't that much reason to read it all because there's very little substance to the world building and it feels tedious. It also doesn't feel like you actually change the course of the game at all as often your dialog options are the same but just worded differently. 

If we look at gameplay: the main missions offer a bunch of ways to get the objective done. That's cool. Outside of that there's no dialog options to talk your way out of things. Stealth is not really rewarded and a lot of it is just combat. The combat in itself is pretty alright but at higher difficulty enemies just become spongy and your weapons generally feel quite weak making a human take as many bullets to the head as a full on robot. For a Saints Row game that's what I'd expect. I was hoping for something a little better here.

Overall with the expectation of an immersive dystopian RPG I can't give it more than a 6/10. It's fun. It works well as 'mindless entertainment' (although admittedly there's to much in the sense of unskipable cutscenes / dialog in the game to be purely that.... just the 'intro' to the game took me 4 hours while not doing that much besides getting to the title screen. Dialog where you don't really have options aside from saying the same thing 2 different ways which in the end doesn't matter).

I think the framework for this game is solid. The art direction is very cool. The music is solid. The factions and stuff that's all good. If they every make a part 2 I hope they invest more into it being an actual RPG more akin to Deus Ex or Mass Effect (although... well controversial ending... but that aside) and that they make it a bit more grounded and gritty.

The game's resurrection from its first release through Phantom Liberty is well documented. A bug filled failure, victim of greed and crunches. But instead of walking away with their tail firmly between their legs, CDPR took the complaints and criticisms to heart, and began a long-term renovation. By patch 1.61, the game actually was playable and you didn't wait for the inevitable crash. With patch 2.0, they rewrote everything from skill trees to fundamental game play. Phantom Liberty may be the only DLC released for the game, but it's one of the best, period. 

The game is based on Mike Pondsmith's TTRPG, and the influence of that game is all over the DNA of 2077. CDPR made changes to fit a video game better, but the fundamental story of living in a world under corporate oppression, the wealthy beyond the law's reach, and survival meaning sometimes giving up on your dreams, remains. The graphics, five years later, are still a benchmark. The story and the characters will draw you in, and your choices often make more of a difference than you think. 

If you can't tell, I love this game. 1300+ hours (and counting), I still find new things every playthrough.

They forgot to put the game in Cyberpunk.

I've been playing through the story for about six hours now, and I think I've seen half an hour of actual gameplay.
The rest of the time has been spent on the intro, endless dialogues, tutorials, driving sequences (which can run on autopilot — no interaction required), and a “Braindance” — which basically means dragging sliders until the game tells you you've done it right.

At times, it feels like you’re playing a one-button game where you’re constantly pressing the “Next” button. This is often the highlighted dialogue option, opening a menu, walking into a trigger, or buying an item. Considering that you’re basically just pressing “Next” the whole time, the key bindings are absolutely bonkers. For example, there are three different buttons for drawing/holstering your weapon on foot and in a vehicle. Why this isn’t just a simple toggle key is beyond me.

You’re constantly forced to wait: Wait for dialogue, wait for the scanner, wait for a cutscene, wait for an elevator, wait until the NPC has walked somewhere. Think I’m exaggerating? Pay attention to how often the current task says something like “wait for … to happen” or how often you’re presented with a progress bar. The only progress bar I expect to see in games Is the loading screen and that should be as quick as possible.

Combat feels both overloaded and one-dimensional at the same time: You’re shown all kinds of stealth and melee mechanics, but you don’t need them at all — you just end up shooting everyone in the face. If you’re playing stealth, the loop goes: Kill, quicksave, kill, quicksave, quickload if you’re spotted, repeat. And then there’s this thing where the game teases you in the intro that you could perform a simultaneous takedown with your companion. Turns out it’s not part of the missions — it only happens when it’s scripted.

The gunplay is somewhat reminiscent of loot shooters like Borderlands, where enemies are bullet sponges and headshots aren’t lethal. Instead, you end up grinding just to get that one upgrade that lets you reload 20% faster—something you should have from the start, so the gameplay isn’t so terribly sluggish. If you can’t take out an enemy from a distance, you just run right up to them and blast them in the face with the shotgun. In any serious shooter, you’d be dead in seconds. But not in Cyberpunk. And this is on Hard. It’s topped off with a bit of hacking, which means you can make enemies explode or stun them just by clicking on them.

Unfortunately, the story hasn't really grabbed me so far either. There are a lot of people who want to hurt you. You die twice. There's a heist, and they implant some stuff in your brain. That's mainly because of the uninteresting characters. We've got Hispano B.J. Blazkovicz and a handful of other plastic buddies, all of whom are way to talkative and never get to the point. If the dialogue options have serious consequences, the game doesn’t convey that very well.
I experienced a bunch of soft locks already where a npc just would not enter his trigger and the mission would not continue.
[Edit ~20h] In the mission "Never Fade Away" I experienced frequent crashes.

It’s all a real shame, because I thought The Witcher 3 was absolutely fantastic.
The lighting is nice, though. Just like the sound design. It can get a little busy at times. But overall, the technical aspects are pretty good.

I’ll keep on playing. If people say the story is good, there must be something to it. Maybe I’ll find the fun at some point. Maybe John Wick will cheer me up. But then again why does it take a game like this 6 hours to present something interesting? I could have played an entire other game with actual interaction at that time.

[Edit at 10 hours]
I found a scene that’s symptomatic of cyberpunk:
In a brothel, you have a conversation with a prostitute. The goal is to get some information. During this conversation, you’re bombarded with calendar quotes:
“You’re scared because you have given up on your dreams.”
“Not a single thing in this world isn’t in the process of becoming something else.”
“Fear is our weapon in the fight against death.”
"But everything has its end."
The conversation is so generic: if you replace V with $Name and Night City with $Location, you could insert it into any series or game. I suspect you’re supposed to learn something about V’s character, but you don’t. What makes this even more absurd is that you can bypass the scene from the very beginning by saying the safeword (even though you are not in an extreme situation). 
What some might call “building atmosphere,” I consider a waste of time. There are so many games that manage to portray deep characters and atmosphere without trapping you in hours of fluff dialogue.

Cyberpunk 2077 is still in 2026 a gorgeous game. Night City looks absolutely stunning and on a modern PC you can crank the graphics settings all the way up and still enjoy an incredibly smooth experience. Your GPU may sound like it's preparing for takeoff, but hey, that's a small price to pay for pretty neon lights.

There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and some of them are genuinely great. That said, I still found myself wishing there were more. Apparently, I have developed an unhealthy appetite for wandering around Night City doing increasingly ridiculous jobs for complete strangers.

The biggest problem, however, is the main story. It's simply too short. If you focus mostly on the main quests, the game ends before it really feels like you've gotten your money's worth. You spend all this time building your character, exploring Night City and becoming murder machine, only for the main story to basically end too soon.

Thankfully, Cyberpunk 2077 has some solid replay value. You can approach the game with completely different builds, whether you want to be a stealthy hacker, a heavily armed psychopath, a katana-wielding lunatic, or some other combination of questionable life choices. Changing your stats and playstyle can make another playthrough feel surpprisingly different.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic-looking and incredibly smooth game with a huge amount of potential content, but I can't help feeling that the main story should have been significantly longer.

Cyberpunk 2077 might be the first game I've played where I genuinely enjoy the characters, world, story and combat while simultaneously wanting to launch the entire installation into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sun.

The vanilla character customization is embarrassingly shallow for a game whose entire setting revolves around modifying the human body. Night City is full of people with cybernetic limbs, mechanical jaws, artificial skin, exposed hardware and insane body modifications. Meanwhile V gets some lines on his face and apparently we're supposed to go, “Yep, I'm a cyborg now.”

So naturally, I went to mods.

That was a mistake.

Want cybernetic arms? Great. Download the arms.

Except you also need a framework.

And another framework.

And a cyberware core.

And an equipment system.

And an Atelier system.

Then you launch the game and discover the store exists BUT THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ARMS AREN'T IN IT because apparently you downloaded the framework for the arms, the store for the arms, the system for equipping the arms, and everything else required to contemplate the philosophical concept of an arm — except the actual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arm.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Now there are six stores.

Four are empty.

WHY ARE THEY THERE?

Install more mods to populate them.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Want gauges? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want facial cyberware? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want clothes that don't look like V dressed himself by blindly sprinting through a futuristic Goodwill? Welcome back to Nexus.

And God help you if you install a giant mod collection hoping somebody else has already assembled all this into a coherent package. I tried that. I ended up with 300+ mods, stores containing nothing, stores containing nothing but shoes, mountains of Fem V cosmetics I couldn't use, dependencies for mods I didn't want, and absolutely no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea which piece of this Jenga tower was responsible for what.

I eventually deleted the collection and discovered I'd spent more time modding Cyberpunk than playing Cyberpunk.

The frustrating part is that underneath all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I actually like the game. I care about these characters. Panam is fantastic. Night City is incredible. When the combat and cyberware fantasy clicks, it's awesome.

That's precisely why this pisses me off so much.

A game called CYBERPUNK should not require an undergraduate degree in ArchiveXL, TweakXL, RED4ext, redscript, Codeware, Equipment-EX, CET, Virtual Atelier and whatever other technological incantation I've forgotten just so my character can LOOK LIKE A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CYBORG.

The modding community has produced some genuinely incredible work, and individual mod authors clearly put enormous effort into it. But the user experience of the Cyberpunk modding ecosystem is atrocious. Dependencies stacked on dependencies, content separated across downloads, storefronts separated from merchandise, inconsistent installation methods, and documentation that frequently assumes you already understand the ecosystem.

After hours of troubleshooting, installing, uninstalling, launching, quitting, relaunching and wondering why another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ store is empty, I have reached enlightenment:

Maybe the real cyberpsychosis was the mods we installed along the way.

10/10 Panam.

9/10 Night City.

2/10 character customization.

0/10 second job as an unpaid Night City systems administrator.

Game just does not feel finished. There are still tons of bugs and I will list a couple of the most common/memorable at the end of my review. 

My three general complaints are: 
1. You level up way to fast to the point where it feels punishing to play the hacker playstyle. Every mission you can kill everybody no matter what by only clicking a few buttons. I do think this is a general game issue because the game feels very easy even on the highest difficulty. The only real challenge is when I tell myself "I will only use [x] weapon for this mission." Some enemies have "resistances" to certain forms of combat, but attaching that to the ram system negates it due to the many ways to regen ram or overcharge mode, which allows you to sacrifice hp to hack increasing your ram pool near infinitely. 
2. I don't know if this is just me, but the main story fails to entertain me. This is okay because the side missions are honestly more fun than the busywork the main missions provide. Too much dialogue, too much following frustratingly slow NPCs, and too many tasks and decisions that feel unimportant. 
3. Lastly I know its hard to make games look good while flying; but having flying cars around, millions of dollars in the bank, and being unable to buy one feels kinda bad for a futuristic game. 

All that being said: The world has amazing atmosphere. Driving around, especially in the rain or at night, feels just amazing. The music, the views, and just something I cant explain gives me a amazing feeling of being small... of peace. I do wish there were driving sounds though. 

Here is a list of bugs I have experienced so far. 
1. Picking up items or opening a chest frequently causes things to go flying.
2. NPCs t-posing while driving their cars.
3. Story NPCs get hit by cars during cutscenes causing their dead bodies to drag on the floor while talking to me until they start a different animation and get revived.
4. Enemies glitching into walls and floors.
5. Enemies seeing you through walls and floors.
6. Once a enemy I killed glitched so hard his body was shot into the sky while his head was stuck on a railing causing his entire model to be a massive tapestry spanning over a block and crashing my FPS till it unloaded.
7. Cyberpsycho missions, while being some of the most fun, are also insanely buggy with their triggers. Three times I have had to fast travel, skip 48 hours in time, and then go back just to have things spawn or trigger.
8. Constant floating items, occasional floating NPCs, and briefly floating cars before they crash down. 

The bugs are the main reason I just cannot recommend this game. They break immersion more than anything else.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a story rich RPG featuring a beautiful open world, with the best character writing I've seen. The game covers themes such as freedom, identity, greed, and social inequality. It's an unforgettable experience worth playing. Jackie Welles & Johnny Silverhand are [b] GOATED [/b] support characters!

Story: You play as V, a lone merc in Night City, a futuristic violent dystopia dictated by greedy capitalist mega-corporations. You take on the most dangerous jobs trying to stay alive and make a name for yourself. There are 3 life paths to choose from: Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo. They don't make much of a difference gameplay-wise, aside from unique dialogue options and shaping V's perspective on the world. After your biggest high stakes job goes FUBAR, the story truly begins as you race against time for your life! 

Gameplay: This game feels like a mixture of GTA and Borderlands because of the interactivity, stores, looting, class building, and the leeway to play however you like. Unfortunately, some elements are not well polished, but its not that bad because they can be fixed with mods. Majority of the cars handle terribly! I got around the map 90% of the time using motorcycles because they're really fast and consistently handle well. Another thing I did not enjoy too much was the early game. Enemies scale heavily to your level at all times, so the beginning is kind of rough because your guns aren't strong and targets feel tanky. Shotguns, revolvers, and snipers became my go to weapons. You'll be fine if your aim and positioning is really good. Mid to late game is when you can really start going crazy. 

Environment: Along with the story, this is another great aspect because of its visual storytelling. It shows you how bad things are, instead of telling you. The city is plagued with advertisements, some even reaching the sky! Gangs rule certain city districts, crime thrives more often in some places, and you can really see the poverty and flourishment of areas. What I truly did love were the small mentions of the 2076 Edgerunners crew. You can find iconic items left behind by a few members which is very cool, it makes the city's history feel more connected on a deeper level.

Side Quests: There are many to do and they give you really good rewards, but they aren't special because they follow a repetitive format. The only good quests are the character story missions, these deepen your bond with key characters, allowing you to learn their history and help them out with personal troubles. 

TL;DR Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best story rich RPG games you can ever play. It has some issues gameplay wise, but they're relatively minor and won't hurt your overall experience. Never stop fighting, my chooms!

The Death of The Cayo Perico Heist: How Rockstar Methodically Killed the Only Fair Content in GTA Online
When The Cayo Perico Heist dropped in December 2020, GTA Online players felt like they could finally breathe. After years of forced cooperative misery, mental breakdowns caused by unreliable random players, and outrageously overpriced properties, Rockstar finally delivered something that felt too good to be true: a highly lucrative heist that could be played entirely solo.

Cayo Perico was the ultimate symbol of freedom in Los Santos. You didn’t have to beg anyone to join, and you didn’t have to waste hours on tedious setups. You could jump in, pull off a slick stealth run, and pocket $1.3 to $1.8 million in just over an hour.

But then, Rockstar realized that players were actually having fun, and—more importantly in their eyes—they weren’t buying Shark Cards anymore. That’s when the methodical, ruthless, and shameless nerfing of the heist began, turning El Rubio's island into a frustrating, low-paying chore.

The Rap Sheet: How a Jackpot Was Turned into Spare Change
1. The Desecration of the Pink Diamond and Primary Targets
We used to cheer when we saw the pink diamond on the security cameras, knowing we were in for a massive payday. Today, Rockstar has practically stripped these targets of their value. Slashing the value of the Pink Diamond—sometimes dragging the total payout of a solo run down toward the $900k mark—is a massive slap in the face to the player's time. Why risk your neck against a private army when you walk away with barely more than what a basic VIP contract used to pay?

2. The Systematic Punishment of Solo Players (The Cooldown Terror)
The most hostile move was the execution of the solo playstyle. If you complete the heist alone, the game now forces a brutal 3-game-day cooldown (approx. 2 hours and 24 minutes) before you can start it again. Meanwhile, team play has a much shorter cooldown. This isn’t "game balance"; it's blatant extortion: “Play with others (who will take a cut of your money), or wait hours to play again.”

3. Guards Suddenly Became Mind-Reading Geniuses (Wallhack AI)
Stealth was the beating heart of Cayo Perico. You followed your memorized route, quietly took out the guards, and slipped away unnoticed. But Rockstar rolled out an update where guards now detect dead bodies. While this sounds good on paper, GTA Online’s notoriously buggy, decade-old AI turned it into a disaster. Guards now frequently see through solid walls or spot corpses on the completely opposite side of the map. Precise stealth has been replaced by a frustrating, unpredictable gamble.

4. Jacked-Up Setup Fees
Just to make absolutely sure you don’t keep too much of your hard-earned cash, they quadrupled the heist setup fee from $25,000 to $100,000. Before you even set foot on the island to scout, you start in the negatives, all while your final payout is actively being gutted.

Verdict: A Monument to Corporate Greed
The current state of the Cayo Perico Heist is a perfect mirror of what GTA Online has become: a game that is no longer designed to entertain you, but to frustrate you into opening your real-world wallet.

They took away the freedom, they took away the fair pay, and they replaced it with a buggy, soul-crushing grind. Rockstar didn't just ruin El Rubio's island; they sabotaged their relationship with their own community. This isn't game development—it's highway robbery.

Its ok. Story was interesting at first but towards the end I was just rushing through to get it over with. Gameplay was whatever. I mostly played with Katanas, maybe that was a bad idea but it was just fine. AI provides no challenge. I recall defeating one boss by circling around a pillar repeatedly while blasting it with headshots each time it froze to T-pose. Enough said there I think. Almost never engaged with the quickhack mechanics, it was easy enough just running up and slicing enemies with my katana. Tried to do a stealth build but I got bored because of the unintelligent AI so I switched to melee/shotguns, which made it less boring.

The world is very pretty and interesting to look at. I never felt particularly interested or encouraged to explore so I never did except to finish quests. I think the only optional content I finished was the Delamaine quest and part of the cyberpycho quests. Very forgettable.

I never felt like my dialogue choices made much difference, especially the skill checks. I don't think those options affected dialogue even a single time. Most irritating example was succeeding a "cool" check to ask a merchant for a discount. They immediately tell me to ♥♥♥♥ off. Why even waste my time?

 I did enjoy dressing up my character quite a bit. It was the only thing I ever spent my money on since the game throws guns at you and I never felt the need to buy a car. It was annoying though because I had to keep driving around to different clothing stores to find clothes I liked.

I expected a lot more from this game. It was all kind of forgettable and never particularly interesting. None of the characters made much of an impression on me except for the arasaka bodyguard (cant remember his name) but I didn't know I could save him so he just died. Modern games have trained me to assume I cant do anything that isn't explicitly told to me by the game, so good on them for having a hidden outcome, but it ended up removing the only character I cared about so R.I.P. I think I got the "good" ending (the aldecaldo ending), but it didn't leave me satisfied (partly because I screwed up hooking up with Panam, my fault). I'd say this game was about as enjoyable as Fallout 4, with a better story and much better character customization.
